title: Terrestrial arthropod community responses to livestock grazing
content:
Our review has highlighted that non-significant or neutral responses of arthropods to grazing are common in the published literature, and that taxonomic and functional approaches may reveal different directional responses. To improve understanding of effects on a broader range of arthropods and community-level processes, we recommend more researchers use sampling methods other than pitfall trapping, and focus on methods that target key functional groups and are appropriate to the ecosystem type. While building a rigorous evidence base on arthropod biodiversity in livestock systems is a priority, management approaches should take a precautionary approach, prioritising heterogeneity and monitoring effects on ecological interactions and functional roles.


Abstract

Livestock grazing is a major land-use globally with a wide range of documented effects on biodiversity. Arthropods are a dominant component of biodiversity in grazed landscapes, but their responses to grazing vary among taxa and ecosystem type. Here, we review and synthesise the global literature on terrestrial arthropod responses to livestock grazing, with the aim to identify trends and knowledge gaps in the literature and recommend research priorities to increase knowledge of how grazing activity by managed livestock influences community-level processes and ecosystem function. We found the majority of studies focused on ground-active arthropods in grassland biomes of the northern hemisphere. Studies using a taxonomic approach typically reported more negative responses than positive, while studies taking a functional approach often reported more positive than negative responses. Very few studies (7%) directly measured grazing effects on a community-level interaction involving insects (e.g. pollination, parasitism, seed dispersal), limiting our broader understanding of how livestock grazing impacts ecological function and processes. Synthesis and Applications: Our review has highlighted that non-significant or neutral responses of arthropods to grazing are common in the published literature, and that taxonomic and functional approaches may reveal different directional responses. To improve understanding of effects on a broader range of arthropods and community-level processes, we recommend more researchers use sampling methods other than pitfall trapping, and focus on methods that target key functional groups and are appropriate to the ecosystem type. While building a rigorous evidence base on arthropod biodiversity in livestock systems is a priority, management approaches should take a precautionary approach, prioritising heterogeneity and monitoring effects on ecological interactions and functional roles.
